summary: This note surveys the history of mosaic art across regions and periods, from late Roman and Byzantine works in Ravenna, Milan and the East to medieval Western church decoration, Umayyad Islamic floor and wall mosaics, and later modern examples. It highlights notable sites such as the Madaba Map, the Hisham's Palace bath mosaic, the Great Mosque of Corduba, and the Iconoclastic-era cross mosaics. The text also notes how fresco and tile gradually supplanted mosaic in some traditions.
one_line: A survey of mosaic art history from Roman and Byzantine works through medieval Europe, Umayyad Islamic art, and modern installations.
key_facts: Later fresco replaced the more labor-intensive technique of mosaic in Western Europe, although mosaics were sometimes used on medieval cathedrals.

The Royal Basilica of the Hungarian kings in Székesfehérvár (Alba Regia) had apse mosaics probably made in the first decades of the 11th century, almost totally destroyed with the basilica in the 17th century.
The Golden Gate of the St. Vitus Cathedral in Prague is named for a golden 14th-century mosaic of the Last Judgement above the portal, executed by Venetian craftsmen.
Ravenna, capital of the Western Roman Empire, became the center of late Roman mosaic art in the following century.

The mosaics in the St Aquilinus Chapel of the Basilica of San Lorenzo in Milan, from the late 4th and early 5th centuries, are outstanding for bright colors, naturalism and adherence to classical canons.
The Cathedral of Spoleto's upper façade has a huge mosaic portraying the Blessing Christ, signed by one Solsternus from 1207.
The Madaba Map was made between 542 and 570 as the floor of the church of Saint George at Madaba, Jordan, and was rediscovered in 1894.
The Madaba Map is the oldest surviving cartographic depiction of the Holy Land, extending from Lebanon in the north to the Nile Delta in the south.
In the Madaba Map, Jerusalem is the largest and most detailed element and sits at the center of the map.
The bath house of Hisham's Palace in Palestine has a superb floor mosaic made around 744, depicting a large tree with a lion attacking a deer and two deer grazing.
At Qastal, near Amman, excavations in 2000 uncovered the earliest known Umayyad mosaics in present-day Jordan, dating probably from the caliphate of Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan (685–705).
The golden mosaics in the mihrab and central dome of the Great Mosque in Corduba were made between 965 and 970 by local craftsmen supervised by a master mosaicist from Constantinople.
The Corduba mosaics were purported to evoke the glamour of the Great Mosque in Damascus, which was lost for the Umayyad family.

During the Iconoclastic era, figural mosaics were condemned as idolatry, and churches such as the Hagia Irene in Constantinople (after 740) got plain gold mosaics with a single great cross in the apse.
The Cathedral Basilica of St. Louis in St. Louis, Missouri, contains the world's largest mosaic installation, according to the note.
